definition: Taken by surprise; startled.
note: Old English onbæc meant 'to the back'. 'Taken aback' was first a sailing term, for a ship whose sails were suddenly pressed back against the mast.
hints: Usually comes after 'taken'.
How a sudden surprise leaves you.

definition: To lower someone in rank or dignity.
note: From Old French, built from a Latin word for 'low'. To abase yourself is to make yourself small in front of someone.
hints: Grovelling does this to you.
It lowers rather than raises.

definition: To become less intense; to die down.
note: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down'. Storms, fevers and anger all abate.
hints: What a storm does as it passes.
The opposite of building up.

definition: A building where monks or nuns live and worship.
note: From Old French abaie, ultimately from the Aramaic abba, 'father', via the title of the man who ran it.
hints: Monks might live in one.
Westminster has a famous one.

definition: The head of a monastery.
note: From Latin abbas, from Aramaic abba, 'father'. The monks' leader was, in name, their father.
hints: Leader of a religious house.
His title once meant 'father'.

definition: To hate something deeply.
note: From Latin abhorrere, 'to shrink back in horror', with the same root as horror.
hints: Stronger than mere dislike.
Shares a root with horror.

definition: To put up with; to tolerate.
note: From Old English abidan, 'to wait'. 'Abode', a place you wait in, comes from the same word.
hints: Often follows 'can't'.
To tolerate, or to obey a rule.

definition: A home; the place where someone lives.
note: Once meant the act of waiting. A place you stay in came to be named after the staying.
hints: A rather grand word for home.
Related to a word meaning to stay.

definition: To stop something before it is finished.
note: From Latin aboriri, 'to miscarry', from ab- 'away' and oriri 'to arise'. Missions and computer tasks are aborted too.
hints: Mission control might shout it.
To call something off part-way.

definition: Concerning; on the subject of.
note: Old English onbutan meant 'on the outside of'. Going around something became talking around it.
hints: What a story is said to be.
Also means roughly, as with numbers.

definition: Higher than; over.
note: From Old English abufan, 'on top'. 'Above board' comes from card players keeping their hands visible over the table.
hints: The opposite of below.
Where the sky is, from the ground.

definition: Cruel or improper treatment, or misuse.
note: From Latin abusus, 'used up' or 'misused'. It began as a word for wrong use before it meant cruelty.
hints: Misuse of something, or someone.
Power can be put to this.

definition: A seemingly bottomless chasm.
note: From Greek abussos, 'bottomless', from a- 'not' and bussos 'depth'.
hints: Nietzsche warned it stares back.
A drop with no visible floor.

definition: The nut of the oak tree.
note: From Old English æcern, originally any wild fruit. The spelling bent towards 'oak' and 'corn' later.
hints: Squirrels bury these.
Great oaks are said to grow from it.

definition: Sharp and bitter in smell or taste.
note: From Latin acer, 'sharp'. It was shaped to look like 'acid' by people who assumed the two were related.
hints: Smoke can have this quality.
It catches the back of your throat.

definition: Someone who performs a role on stage or screen.
note: From Latin, 'a doer', from agere 'to do'. In law it once meant the person who brings a case.
hints: Works with scripts and directors.
Plays someone they are not.

definition: Severe and sudden; or sharp.
note: From Latin acutus, 'sharpened'. An acute angle is a sharp one, and an acute illness strikes quickly.
hints: Describes an angle under ninety degrees.
Sudden and severe, in medicine.

definition: An old saying held to be true.
note: From Latin adagium, a proverb. 'A stitch in time' is one.
hints: A proverb by another name.
Old wisdom in a short sentence.

definition: To change to suit new conditions.
note: From Latin adaptare, 'to fit to'. Darwin's species and novels turned into films both do it.
hints: What species do to survive.
A book may be this for the screen.

definition: Very skilled at something.
note: From Latin adeptus, 'having attained'. Alchemists used it of anyone who had cracked the secret of gold.
hints: Highly skilled.
Alchemists claimed the title.

definition: Administrative work; the paperwork side of things.
note: A clipping of administration. On the internet it also names whoever runs a forum or server.
hints: Forms, filing and emails.
The person who can ban you from a server.

definition: To confess; or to let someone in.
note: From Latin admittere, 'to send to'. A ticket admits you; a guilty person admits fault.
hints: What a ticket does at the door.
To own up to something.

definition: Sun-dried brick made of clay and straw.
note: From Spanish, via Arabic, from a Coptic word for brick, which goes back to ancient Egyptian. Few English words are older.
hints: Common building material in the American Southwest.
Mud brick dried in the sun.

definition: To take on as your own.
note: From Latin adoptare, 'to choose for oneself', from optare 'to choose'.
hints: Parents may do this with a child.
You can also do it with an idea.

definition: To love and admire deeply.
note: From Latin adorare, 'to speak to', meaning to pray. It was a word for worship before it was a word for fondness.
hints: Stronger than like.
Once meant to worship.

definition: To decorate or make beautiful.
note: From Latin adornare, 'to furnish', the same root as ornate and ornament.
hints: What jewellery does to a person.
Related to ornament.

definition: A fully grown person or animal.
note: From Latin adultus, 'grown up'. Adolescent comes from the same verb: one is growing, the other has grown.
hints: No longer a child.
Shares a root with adolescent.

definition: To attach; or a prefix or suffix.
note: From Latin affixus, 'fastened to'. Grammar borrowed it for the bits fastened onto words.
hints: Un- and -ness are examples.
To stick one thing to another.

definition: On fire.
note: Simply a- 'on' plus fire, like ablaze. It is used about passions as often as buildings.
hints: Burning, in a literary way.
A heart might be described this way.

definition: Happening or being planned.
note: Literally 'on foot'. Sherlock Holmes made 'the game is afoot' famous, borrowing it from Shakespeare.
hints: Holmes says the game is this.
Something is being planned.

definition: In conflict with; in trouble with.
note: From a- plus foul. Ships ran afoul of each other when their rigging tangled.
hints: Usually followed by 'of the law'.
Tangled up in trouble.

definition: Later than; following.
note: From Old English æfter. 'Aftermath' first meant a second crop of grass mown after the first.
hints: The opposite of before.
Comes later in time.

definition: Once more.
note: From Old English ongean, 'back'. 'Against' grew from the same word.
hints: One more time.
Encore means roughly this.

definition: With the mouth wide open in wonder.
note: A- plus gape. Its first known use is in Milton's Paradise Lost, in 1667.
hints: Jaw hanging open.
Milton is credited with it.

definition: A banded, semi-precious stone.
note: From Greek achates, named after the river in Sicily where the stone was found.
hints: Marbles were once made of it.
A banded gemstone.

definition: Someone who acts on another's behalf.
note: From Latin agens, 'doing'. A secret agent and a chemical agent both make things happen.
hints: Spies and estate brokers are both called this.
Someone who acts for you.

definition: Able to move quickly and easily.
note: From Latin agilis, 'nimble', from agere 'to drive'. Software teams adopted it in 2001.
hints: Gymnasts and goats are this.
Quick on your feet.

definition: Glowing with light, warmth or happiness.
note: A- plus glow, like afire and ablaze. Faces are aglow as often as fires.
hints: Lit up warmly.
A happy face might be this.

definition: Extreme physical or mental pain.
note: From Greek agonia, 'struggle', from agon, an athletic contest. The pain came from the effort.
hints: Severe suffering.
Its Greek root meant a contest.

definition: A public square or market in ancient Greece.
note: Greek for 'gathering place'. Agoraphobia is a fear of open, public spaces.
hints: Athenians gathered here.
Hidden in a word for fearing crowds.

definition: To share an opinion.
note: From Old French a gré, 'to one's liking', from Latin gratum, 'pleasing'.
hints: What two people do when they see eye to eye.
Nodding usually signals it.

definition: In front; in the future.
note: A- plus head, probably first a sailor's word for beyond the ship's bow.
hints: Further forward.
The opposite of behind.

definition: A passage between rows of seats or shelves.
note: From Old French ele, 'wing', from Latin ala. It meant the side wings of a church before it meant a walkway.
hints: Supermarkets and planes have them.
Brides walk down one.

definition: A warning of danger, or the device that sounds it.
note: From Italian all'arme, 'to arms!', the cry raised when an enemy appeared.
hints: It wakes you in the morning.
Once a call to grab weapons.

definition: A collection of recordings, or a book for photos.
note: Latin for a blank white tablet, from albus 'white'. Romans posted public notices on one.
hints: Musicians release these.
Its Latin root meant white.

definition: Watchful and ready.
note: From Italian all'erta, 'on the lookout', from erta, a high lookout post.
hints: Fully awake and watchful.
Lifeguards should be this.

definition: Simple water plants such as seaweed and pond scum.
note: Plural of Latin alga, 'seaweed'. They produce much of the oxygen in the air.
hints: Turns a pond green.
Seaweed belongs here.

definition: A being from another world; or anything foreign.
note: From Latin alienus, 'belonging to another', from alius, 'other'.
hints: Science fiction is full of them.
From somewhere else entirely.

definition: To bring into a line.
note: From French aligner, from Latin linea, 'line'. Text, wheels and stars can all be aligned.
hints: What you do with text in a document.
To line things up.

definition: Similar; in the same way.
note: From Old English gelic, 'similar', related to the word like.
hints: Twins often look this way.
Similar to each other.

definition: Living; not dead.
note: From Old English on life, literally 'in life'. The a- in many such words is a worn-down 'on'.
hints: The opposite of dead.
Full of energy, or simply breathing.

definition: To calm or lessen a fear or worry.
note: From Old English alecgan, 'to lay down'. You lay a fear to rest.
hints: What reassurance does to fears.
To put a worry to rest.

definition: A narrow passage between buildings.
note: From Old French alee, 'a going', from aller 'to go'. A bowling alley is a long narrow lane too.
hints: Cats and bins live in one.
Bowling happens in one.

definition: To give out as a share.
note: From Old French aloter, 'to divide by lot'. Shares were once settled by drawing lots.
hints: What you do with time or seats.
To share out portions.

definition: To let something happen.
note: From Old French alouer, which blended two Latin verbs, one for praise and one for placing.
hints: To give permission.
Parents decide what to do this with.

definition: A metal made by mixing two or more metals.
note: From Old French aloi, from a Latin word for binding together. Bronze is copper and tin.
hints: Brass and bronze are examples.
Metals melted together.

definition: Up in the air.
note: From Old Norse a lopti, 'in the sky'. Sailors used it for anything up the mast.
hints: Up in the rigging, to a sailor.
Held up high.

definition: By yourself.
note: From all plus one, 'wholly one'. 'Lonely' was later formed from it by dropping the a-.
hints: Without company.
'Lonely' was clipped from it.

definition: Moving in a line beside something.
note: From Old English andlang, 'extending opposite'. You walk along a beach.
hints: How you walk a riverbank.
Coming with others: tagging this.

definition: Distant and cool towards others.
note: A sailing term: to keep a ship's head 'a loof', to windward, away from the shore.
hints: Standoffish.
Its root is a sailing command.

definition: In a voice others can hear.
note: Simply a- plus loud. Reading aloud was normal; silent reading once astonished people.
hints: Not silently.
How you read to a child.

definition: The first letter of the Greek alphabet.
note: From Phoenician aleph, 'ox', whose letter was drawn as an ox head. Turn our A upside down and you can still see the horns.
hints: Comes before beta.
Software releases begin with it.

definition: A table used for religious offerings or ceremonies.
note: From Latin altare, likely related to altus, 'high'. Weddings take place in front of one.
hints: Couples stand before one to marry.
A raised table in a church.

definition: To change.
note: From Latin alter, 'the other'. Altering something makes it other than it was.
hints: Tailors do it to trousers.
To make different.

definition: To gather a large amount.
note: From French amasser, 'to heap up', from masse, 'mass'.
hints: What hoarders do with things.
To pile up over time.

definition: To astonish.
note: Middle English amasen meant to bewilder. 'Maze' is the same word: a place made to bewilder you.
hints: What magicians aim to do.
Related to a puzzle of paths.

definition: Fossilised tree resin, or its golden-orange colour.
note: From Arabic anbar, which first meant ambergris from whales. The name slid onto the resin.
hints: Insects are found trapped in it.
The middle traffic light.

definition: To walk slowly and easily.
note: From Old French ambler, 'to walk like a horse', from Latin ambulare 'to walk'.
hints: A relaxed stroll.
Ambulance shares its root.

definition: To change to make better.
note: From Latin emendare, 'to remove a fault'. The US Constitution has twenty-seven of them.
hints: Constitutions get these.
To correct a text.

definition: Wrong or out of place.
note: A- plus miss. 'Something is amiss' means something has missed its mark.
hints: Something is not right.
Often follows 'something is'.

definition: Friendly relations.
note: From Old French amistie, from Latin amicus, 'friend'.
hints: Friendship between nations.
Its Latin root is friend.

definition: Surrounded by; in the company of.
note: From Old English on gemang, 'in a crowd'.
hints: In the middle of a group.
Similar to amid.

definition: More than enough.
note: From Latin amplus, 'large, spacious'. Amplify comes from the same root.
hints: Plenty, with room to spare.
Related to amplify.

definition: In a way that is more than enough.
note: From ample, from Latin amplus, 'large'. To be amply rewarded is to get plenty.
hints: Generously or fully.
How a debt might be repaid.

definition: To make someone laugh or smile.
note: From Old French amuser, 'to divert attention'. It first meant to fool or distract someone.
hints: What a clown tries to do.
Its old meaning was to distract.

definition: A heavenly messenger.
note: From Greek angelos, 'messenger'. Angels were defined by their job, carrying word from God.
hints: Tops many Christmas trees.
Its Greek root meant messenger.

definition: A strong feeling of displeasure.
note: From Old Norse angr, 'grief'. It meant sorrow before it meant rage.
hints: What a temper unleashes.
Seeing red is this.

definition: The space between two lines that meet.
note: From Latin angulus, 'corner'. Angling for fish comes from a different word meaning hook.
hints: Measured in degrees.
A protractor measures it.

definition: Feeling or showing anger.
note: From anger, which in Old Norse meant grief or trouble.
hints: Cross, or worse than cross.
How you feel when wronged.

definition: Japanese animated film and television.
note: A Japanese clipping of the English 'animation'. English borrowed the clipped word back.
hints: Studio Ghibli makes it.
Animation from Japan.

definition: The joint between the foot and the leg.
note: From Old English ancleow. The bones were once compared to an angle or bend.
hints: Easy to twist.
Where a sock ends.

definition: An extra building attached to a main one; or to take over territory.
note: From Latin annexus, 'joined to'. Countries annex land; hotels have annexes.
hints: An extension of a building.
What empires do to land.

definition: To irritate.
note: From Old French anoier, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred'. Ennui shares the root.
hints: What a buzzing fly does.
Shares a root with ennui.

definition: To declare legally invalid.
note: From Latin annullare, 'to make nothing', from nullus.
hints: What can happen to a marriage.
Related to null.

definition: The positive electrode of a battery or cell.
note: Coined in 1834 for Michael Faraday, from Greek ana 'up' and hodos 'way'.
hints: Partner of the cathode.
Faraday asked for the word.

definition: Playful and silly behaviour.
note: From Italian antico, 'ancient', used for the strange creatures painted on Roman walls.
hints: Usually plural: silly capers.
Grotesque old paintings gave it its name.

definition: A heavy iron block on which metal is hammered.
note: From Old English anfilt, 'something beaten on'. One of the ear's tiny bones is named after it.
hints: A blacksmith's essential.
Cartoon villains drop these.

definition: The main artery leaving the heart.
note: From Greek aorte, 'that which is hung up'. Aristotle named it.
hints: The body's largest artery.
Carries blood away from the heart.

definition: Separated by distance.
note: From French a part, 'to the side'.
hints: Not together.
How couples feel when separated.

definition: A small sap-sucking insect.
note: Linnaeus coined aphis in 1758, possibly misreading the Greek word for bug.
hints: Ladybirds eat them.
A garden pest on roses.

definition: A temporary pause in breathing, often during sleep.
note: From Greek apnoia, 'without breath'.
hints: A sleep disorder.
Breathing stops for a while.

definition: A round fruit with crisp flesh.
note: Old English æppel meant any fruit. The fruit in Eden is never named as an apple.
hints: Keeps the doctor away.
Newton watched one fall.

definition: To put on; or to request formally.
note: From Latin applicare, 'to fold onto'. You apply paint, and apply for a job.
hints: You do it for a job.
What you do with sunscreen.

definition: A garment worn over clothes to keep them clean.
note: Originally 'a napron'. People heard 'an apron', and the n moved across. Napkin keeps it.
hints: Worn while cooking.
It lost its first letter to 'an'.

definition: In a fitting way.
note: From apt, from Latin aptus, 'fitted'.
hints: Done in a fitting way.
How a well-chosen name suits.

definition: A shady garden shelter covered in climbing plants.
note: From Old French erbier, 'herb garden'. People later linked it to Latin arbor, 'tree'.
hints: Vines and roses climb it.
A shady garden nook.

definition: An enclosed area for sport or shows.
note: Latin for 'sand'. Roman arenas were strewn with it to soak up the blood.
hints: Gladiators fought in one.
Its Latin root meant sand.

definition: To disagree with words.
note: From Latin arguere, 'to make clear'. It was once about proving a point, not fighting.
hints: What lawyers do in court.
Not quite agreeing.

definition: To come into being; to get up.
note: From Old English arisan, 'to rise'.
hints: What problems tend to do.
To stand up, in older English.

definition: Protective covering worn in battle.
note: From Latin armatura, 'equipment', from arma, 'weapons'.
hints: Knights clanked in it.
Shares a root with army.

definition: A distinctive, usually pleasant smell.
note: From Greek aroma, 'spice'. In Latin it was used in the plural for spices and sweet herbs.
hints: Coffee and fresh bread have one.
A pleasant smell drifting out.

definition: An impressive range or display of things.
note: From Old French areer, 'to put in order'. Programmers use it for an ordered list of values.
hints: A wide, orderly display.
A list of values, to a programmer.

definition: A pointed shaft shot from a bow.
note: From Old English earh. Its shape now points the way on every sign and screen.
hints: Cupid fires them.
A bow sends it flying.

definition: The crime of deliberately setting fire to property.
note: From Old French arsoun, from Latin ardere, 'to burn'. Ardent shares the root.
hints: A crime involving fire.
Investigators look for accelerants.

definition: Showily artistic or bohemian.
note: An American form of arty, from arts plus -y. Often said with a slight eye-roll.
hints: Like a beret-wearing gallery crowd.
Arty, with an eye-roll.

definition: A wide silk tie looped under the chin.
note: Named after Royal Ascot, the racecourse where fashionable men wore them.
hints: A cravat by another name.
Named after a racecourse.

definition: Pale grey, especially from shock or illness.
note: From ash plus -en, 'made of ash'. Faces turn ashen with fright.
hints: How a frightened face looks.
The colour of something burnt out.

definition: To one side; or a remark made quietly.
note: From Old English on side. In theatre, an aside is spoken to the audience, unheard by the others on stage.
hints: Actors speak one to the audience.
Out of the way.

definition: Not straight; crooked.
note: A- plus skew. A picture on a wall can hang this way.
hints: Not hanging straight.
Wonky, off-kilter.

definition: A test of a metal's purity.
note: From Old French assai, 'trial'. Essay comes from the same word: an essay is an attempt.
hints: Gold is tested this way.
Shares a root with essay.

definition: A ring-shaped coral island around a lagoon.
note: From Dhivehi, the language of the Maldives, where the country is made of them.
hints: A ring of coral.
The Maldives are built of them.

definition: To make amends for a wrong.
note: From 'at one'. To atone was to bring two sides into harmony again.
hints: Make up for a sin.
Literally 'at one'.

definition: The space just below a roof.
note: From Attica, the region around Athens: its architectural style used a decorated top storey.
hints: Old boxes are stored up there.
Named after the region around Athens.

definition: An official check of accounts.
note: From Latin auditus, 'hearing'. Accounts were once read aloud to the examiner.
hints: Accountants dread or perform it.
Its root means hearing.

definition: To be a sign of what will happen.
note: A Roman augur foretold the future from the flight of birds. Inauguration began with one.
hints: Things may bode well or ill this way.
Romans read birds to do it.

definition: An aunt, or an affectionate name for an older woman.
note: A pet form of aunt. In many cultures it is used for any respected older woman.
hints: Your parent's sister.
A fond name for an older woman.

definition: Use or benefit.
note: From Old French valoir, 'to be worth'. 'To no avail' means it did no good.
hints: Usually 'to no ...'.
Of use or help.

definition: To turn away; to prevent.
note: From Latin avertere, 'to turn from'. You avert your eyes, or a disaster.
hints: What you do with your eyes from a horror.
To stop something bad happening.

definition: Relating to birds.
note: From Latin avis, 'bird'. Aviation comes from the same root.
hints: Bird flu is this kind of influenza.
Related to aviation.

definition: To stay away from.
note: From Old French esvuidier, 'to empty out'. Void shares the root.
hints: What you do with an ex in the street.
To steer clear.

definition: To wait for.
note: From Old French awaitier, 'to lie in wait'.
hints: What you do for news.
A grand way to wait.

definition: Not asleep.
note: From Old English awacan, 'to arise'. Two older verbs, one for waking up and one for being up, merged into it.
hints: The opposite of asleep.
Eyes open in the morning.

definition: A prize given for achievement.
note: From Old French awarder, 'to observe, then decide'. It began as a judge's decision.
hints: An Oscar is one.
A prize or ruling.

definition: Knowing about something.
note: From Old English gewær, 'watchful'. Wary shares the root.
hints: Conscious of something.
Related to wary.

definition: Flooded or covered with water.
note: A- plus wash. A rock is awash when waves just cover it.
hints: Flooded, literally or with something.
A city might be this with tourists.

definition: Very bad.
note: Awe plus -ful. It once meant full of awe, inspiring wonder, before it slid to dreadful.
hints: Terrible, or very bad.
It once meant inspiring wonder.

definition: Relating to an axis.
note: From Latin axis, 'axle'. An axial line runs down the centre of something.
hints: Along a central line.
The Earth's tilt is this.

definition: A statement accepted as true without proof.
note: From Greek axioma, 'what is thought worthy'. Euclid's geometry is built on five.
hints: A self-evident truth.
Euclid started from them.

definition: A proposed subatomic particle.
note: Coined by physicist Frank Wilczek in 1978, who named it after a brand of laundry detergent because it 'cleaned up' a problem.
hints: A hypothetical particle.
Named after a laundry detergent.

definition: Bright blue, like a clear sky.
note: From Arabic lazaward, 'lapis lazuli', the blue stone. The first letter fell off in Old French.
hints: The colour of a cloudless sky.
Named after a blue stone.

definition: Cured meat from the back and sides of a pig.
note: From Old French bacon, 'back meat'. Bringing home the bacon first meant winning a prize.
hints: Sizzles in a breakfast pan.
Sizzling slices of pork.

definition: A small sign worn to show identity or achievement.
note: Of uncertain origin; first used for heraldic symbols showing whose household you served.
hints: Scouts sew them on sleeves.
A police officer shows one.

definition: In a poor or unsatisfactory way.
note: Bad plus -ly. To want something badly is to want it very much.
hints: Not well at all.
How you want something you crave.

definition: A ring-shaped bread roll, boiled then baked.
note: From Yiddish beygl, from a German word for ring or bracelet.
hints: Often eaten with cream cheese.
A bread roll with a hole.

definition: Loose and hanging away from the body.
note: Bag plus -y. Baggy jeans had a revival in the nineties and again in the 2020s.
hints: Not tight-fitting.
Nineties jeans were this.

definition: Someone who makes bread and cakes.
note: From Old English bæcere. A baker's dozen is thirteen, an extra loaf against short weight.
hints: Works at dawn with ovens.
Their dozen is thirteen.

definition: A machine that packs hay or straw into bales.
note: From bale, a bundle. Farmers tow them behind tractors.
hints: Farm machine for hay.
Turns loose straw into blocks.

definition: Pleasantly warm.
note: From balm, a soothing ointment. A balmy evening soothes like one.
hints: Warm summer evenings are this.
Soothingly mild weather.

definition: Boring and unoriginal.
note: From Old French ban, 'compulsory feudal service'. Shared by everyone, so commonplace.
hints: Trite and predictable.
Common to the point of boredom.

definition: A stringed instrument with a round drum-like body.
note: Brought to America by enslaved West Africans, from an instrument like the akonting.
hints: Bluegrass leans on its twang.
Has a drum-like body.

definition: A flat-bottomed boat for carrying goods on rivers.
note: From Old French barge, via Latin barca, 'small boat'. To barge in is to push in clumsily.
hints: Floats slowly down a canal.
To push rudely into a room.

definition: A nobleman of the lowest rank; or a powerful businessman.
note: From Old French barun, 'man, warrior'. Robber barons were the ruthless tycoons of the 1800s.
hints: Media or oil tycoons are called this.
The lowest rank of peer.

definition: Forming the base; fundamental.
note: From base. Your basal metabolic rate is what your body burns at rest.
hints: At the base of something.
A metabolic rate at rest.

definition: An aromatic herb used in cooking.
note: From Greek basilikon, 'royal'. It was considered a herb fit for kings.
hints: Key in pesto.
Its Greek name meant royal.

definition: A bowl for washing, or a large dip in land.
note: From Old French bacin, from Latin baccinum, 'water vessel'.
hints: A sink is one.
A river drains into one.

definition: The foundation or starting point for something.
note: From Greek basis, 'step' or 'pedestal'. Base shares the root.
hints: Facts form this for an argument.
The grounds for something.

definition: A quantity made at one time.
note: From Old English, 'something baked'. A batch was first the bread from a single firing.
hints: Cookies come out of the oven in one.
A group made together.

definition: To wash in water, or swim.
note: From Old English baþian. Sunbathing borrowed it for lying in light.
hints: To soak in water.
Sunlight can do it to a room.

definition: A short stick used by a conductor, relay runner or officer.
note: From French bâton, 'stick'. Passing the baton means handing over responsibility.
hints: Relay runners pass it.
A conductor waves it.

definition: Slightly mad.
note: From 'bats in the belfry', for a head full of fluttering thoughts.
hints: Eccentric, a bit dotty.
Bats in the belfry.

definition: Humorously rude about sex.
note: From bawd, an old word for a brothel keeper. Shakespeare's comedies are full of bawdy jokes.
hints: Like a saucy seaside postcard.
Rude in a cheerful way.

definition: A slow, marshy creek in the southern United States.
note: From Louisiana French, from Choctaw bayuk, 'creek'.
hints: Louisiana is full of them.
Alligators drift through one.

definition: A sandy or pebbly shore.
note: From Old English bæce, 'stream'. It came to mean the shingle by the water, then the whole shore.
hints: Where sandcastles get built.
Sand, towels and waves.

definition: Small, round and gleaming, like beads.
note: Bead plus -y. 'Keeping a beady eye' on something means watching it closely.
hints: Describes a suspicious bird's eyes.
Watching closely: a ... eye.

definition: Hair growing on the chin and cheeks.
note: From Old English beard. To beard someone once meant to confront them face to face.
hints: Grows on a chin.
Santa has a white one.

definition: A large wild animal; or a brutal person.
note: From Latin bestia, 'animal'. Bestial and beastly share it.
hints: Beauty's companion.
A wild creature.

definition: A tree with smooth grey bark.
note: From Old English bece. Book may share an ancient root, perhaps from runes carved on beech tablets.
hints: A smooth-barked tree.
Its wood may have given us book.

definition: Muscular and solid.
note: Beef plus -y. It moved from meat to muscle to anything robust.
hints: A bodybuilder looks this way.
Bulky and strong.

definition: To be suitable for.
note: Be- plus fit. 'As befits a king' means as is proper for one.
hints: Suitable to someone's status.
Often 'as ... a queen'.

definition: To father a child; or to cause.
note: From Old English begietan, 'to get'. Biblical family lists are long chains of it.
hints: Violence is said to do this to violence.
Old word for fathering.

definition: To start.
note: From Old English beginnan, of uncertain deeper origin.
hints: Opposite of finish.
What you do at the start.

definition: A living creature; or existence.
note: Formed from be plus -ing around the 1300s.
hints: Humans and aliens are both these.
Existence itself.

definition: To let gas out from the stomach noisily.
note: From Old English bealcian, an imitation of the sound.
hints: A burp, more loudly.
Chimneys do it with smoke too.

definition: To give a false impression of.
note: Old English belecgan, 'to surround', later 'to tell lies about'.
hints: A calm face may do this to nerves.
To disguise or contradict.

definition: A beautiful woman, especially the most admired at a party.
note: French for 'beautiful'. 'The belle of the ball' is the night's star.
hints: Of the ball, traditionally.
French for beautiful.

definition: The stomach area of the body.
note: From Old English belg, 'bag'. Bellows shares the root.
hints: A certain kind of dancer moves it.
Related to bellows.

definition: Lower than; under.
note: Be- plus low. Sailors go below to leave the deck.
hints: The opposite of above.
Under something.

definition: A long seat for several people.
note: From Old English benc. Judges sit on one, so 'the bench' means judges.
hints: Parks are full of them.
Players wait on it during a match.

definition: A soft, round, flat cap.
note: From French béret, from a Gascon word for cap.
hints: Classic headwear for French painters.
A soft flat hat.

definition: A small, juicy fruit.
note: From Old English berie. Botanists count bananas as berries and strawberries as not.
hints: Bananas count as one, botanically.
Small, juicy and often red.

definition: A bed on a ship or train; or a ship's mooring place.
note: Possibly from bear, as in the room needed to steer clear. 'Give a wide berth' means keep away.
hints: Give someone a wide one.
A bunk on a ship.

definition: To trouble persistently.
note: From Old English besettan, 'to surround'. A city could be beset by enemies.
hints: Troubles do it from all sides.
Plagued by problems.

definition: A leaf or nut chewed as a stimulant in South and Southeast Asia.
note: From Portuguese, from Malayalam vettila. Chewing it stains the teeth red.
hints: Chewed across South Asia.
Stains the mouth red.

definition: A sloping edge.
note: From Old French baivel, from bayer, 'to gape'. Mirrors often have them.
hints: A slanted edge on glass.
Mirrors are often given one.

definition: The ring holding the glass of a watch or a gem.
note: From French biseau, 'sloping edge'.
hints: Frames a watch face.
Holds a gemstone in place.

definition: An authoritative book on a subject.
note: From Greek biblia, 'books'. 'The angler's bible' borrows the idea of the definitive text.
hints: A must-have reference book.
Its Greek root means books.

definition: The muscle at the front of the upper arm.
note: From Latin biceps, 'two-headed', for its two attachment points. Bicep is a modern back-formation.
hints: Flexed to show strength.
Its Latin root meant two-headed.

definition: A fussy or gossipy old woman.
note: From Biddy, a pet form of Bridget. It became slang for any older woman.
hints: An old busybody.
From a pet form of Bridget.

definition: An intolerant person with fixed prejudices.
note: From French bigot. A popular story traces it to Normans swearing 'bi God', but nobody is sure.
hints: Intolerant of others' views.
Narrow-minded to a fault.

definition: The bottom of a ship's hull; or nonsense.
note: Probably a variant of bulge. The water that collects there is foul, hence nonsense.
hints: Dirty water at the bottom of a ship.
Rubbish talk.

definition: A game of chance played with numbered cards.
note: Probably from bing, a ringing sound. It is also shouted when something works out.
hints: Two little ducks, twenty-two.
Shouted when you win.

definition: A large natural community, such as desert or rainforest.
note: Bio- plus -ome, coined by ecologists in 1916.
hints: The tundra is one.
A large ecological community.

definition: The start of life.
note: From Old Norse byrth. Bear, as in to carry a child, shares the root.
hints: Celebrated each year afterward.
The start of a life.

definition: A large wild ox with a shaggy mane.
note: From Latin bison, a Germanic word for wild ox.
hints: Roamed the great plains.
Often called a buffalo.

definition: Made up of small, unconnected bits.
note: Bit plus -y. Itty-bitty adds a rhyme for extra smallness.
hints: Disjointed, in fragments.
Itty plus it means tiny.

definition: The darkest colour.
note: From Old English blæc. Old English blac, 'pale, shining', was a different word.
hints: Night's colour.
The colour of soot.

definition: The cutting edge of a knife or tool.
note: From Old English blæd, 'leaf'. A blade of grass kept the older sense.
hints: A knife's sharp part.
A single leaf of grass.

definition: Responsibility for a fault.
note: From Old French blasmer, from the same Latin as blaspheme.
hints: What you place on someone.
Related to blaspheme.

definition: Lacking flavour or interest.
note: From Latin blandus, 'smooth, flattering'. It moved from soothing to dull.
hints: Unseasoned food.
Unremarkable.

definition: Empty; with nothing written.
note: From French blanc, 'white'. A blank page was a white one.
hints: A form left unfilled.
Its French root meant white.

definition: To make a loud harsh sound.
note: From Middle English bleren, 'to wail', imitating the noise.
hints: What car horns do.
Music played far too loud.

definition: An explosion or strong gust.
note: From Old English blæst, 'blowing'. As slang, a great time.
hints: A loud explosion.
A really fun time.

definition: A large, fierce fire.
note: From Old English blæse, 'torch'. To blaze a trail meant marking trees by cutting away bark.
hints: A raging fire.
To mark a new trail.

definition: Cold, bare and depressing.
note: From Old Norse bleikr, 'pale'. Bleach shares the root.
hints: A grey winter moor.
Related to bleach.

definition: The cry of a sheep or goat.
note: From Old English blætan, imitating the sound.
hints: What a lamb does.
To complain in a whiny voice.

definition: To lose blood.
note: From Old English bledan, from blod, 'blood'.
hints: What a cut does.
Colours can do it in the wash.

definition: A short high electronic sound.
note: Imitative. TV used it to cover swear words.
hints: Censors put it over swearing.
A short beep.

definition: To mix together.
note: From Old Norse blanda, 'to mix'. Blond may share the root.
hints: What a smoothie maker does.
A mixture of coffees.

definition: To make holy, or to wish someone well.
note: From Old English bletsian, 'to consecrate with blood', from an old sense of sprinkling or marking. Over time the word lost the blood and kept the holiness.
hints: What you might say after someone sneezes.
A priest might do this to a crowd with a raised hand.

definition: A large, rounded airship with no rigid frame.
note: Historians are unsure of its origin, but a popular theory says it imitates the sound made by thumping the airship's skin.
hints: It floats above stadiums, sometimes carrying a camera.
Cousin of the zeppelin, but squashier.

definition: Unable to see.
note: From Old English blind, a very old Germanic word. It also came to describe things you cannot see through, as with window shades.
hints: Window coverings that roll or slat are named for it.
A person who reads with their fingertips, perhaps.

definition: To close and open your eyes quickly.
note: From Middle English blynken, related to an Old English word meaning 'to deceive'. An older sense was a quick glance or gleam of light.
hints: You do it without thinking, thousands of times a day.
A staring contest is lost when you do this.

definition: Perfect happiness.
note: From Old English bliss, from a word for joy. It was once spelled blis and tied to the idea of gladness or a blithe spirit.
hints: A feeling beyond mere contentment.
Ignorance is said to be this.

definition: A sudden, overwhelming attack or burst of effort.
note: Clipped from German Blitzkrieg, 'lightning war'. The German word for lightning is Blitz, and English borrowed it as a name for fast attacks.
hints: Football teams use one to rush the quarterback.
London endured a long wartime one of these from the air.

definition: To swell up with fluid or gas.
note: Perhaps from Middle English blout, 'soft, flexible', from Old Norse. It first meant soft or puffy before it meant swollen.
hints: How you feel after an enormous meal.
Software with too many unneeded features is said to suffer from it.

definition: A man, especially an ordinary one.
note: Its origin is unknown; guesses include Celtic borrowings. It is especially common in British, Australian and Irish English.
hints: A very British word for a guy.
'A decent one', you might say of a friendly fellow.

definition: Having pale yellow hair.
note: Borrowed from French, from Old French blont, which came from a Frankish word for a mixed golden colour. The spelling blond is for male hair; the form with an extra e was for female.
hints: Colour of hair that sunshine might lighten.
Dark-haired people sometimes dye their hair this way.

definition: The red liquid pumped around the body by the heart.
note: From Old English blod, a very old Germanic word. It also came to stand for family ties, as in 'bad' or 'blue' kinds.
hints: Flows through your veins.
What you donate in a drive at the hospital.

definition: Not sharp; or speaking in a direct, tactless way.
note: From Middle English, possibly Old Norse in origin, linked to a verb meaning 'to shut the eyes'. First used of dull edges, later of dull minds and then plain-speaking people.
hints: A knife that cannot cut well is this.
Honest to the point of rudeness.

definition: To say something suddenly, without thinking.
note: Possibly imitative of a sudden sound. It has been used for hasty speech for centuries.
hints: A secret often escapes this way.
Done by someone who can't hold back an answer.

definition: To turn red in the face from embarrassment.
note: From Middle English blusshen, from Old English blysċan, 'to be red, to shine'. A glance or glow of red once described a sudden look as well.
hints: Compliments might make you do it.
Also a pink cosmetic for the cheeks.

definition: A long flat piece of wood.
note: From Old English bord, meaning a plank. It grew into a table, meals ('room and board'), a ship's side, and a group of directors around a table.
hints: What you do to get onto a plane or ship.
Chess and Monopoly are played on one.

definition: One of a pair of small drums played with the hands.
note: From Spanish bongo, the name of these drums of Cuban origin. The same word names a striped African antelope.
hints: Played by hand, usually in pairs.
A beatnik might drum on one.

definition: An extra reward on top of what you expected.
note: Borrowed from Latin bonus, 'good'. It came to mean a good thing added on, such as extra pay.
hints: Paid at year end if the company did well.
An extra level in a video game might be called this.

definition: A silly person; also a tropical seabird.
note: From Spanish bobo, 'fool', from Latin balbus, 'stammering'. The seabird was so named because it seemed foolishly tame and easy to catch.
hints: A trap rigged to catch someone off guard has this word before it.
A bird with blue feet is named for it.

definition: To push up or increase something.
note: Of unknown origin, first recorded in the early 1800s. It started as a push upward for someone climbing.
hints: What a pep talk gives to morale.
A helping hand to lift you up.

definition: A small enclosed stall or compartment.
note: From a Norse word meaning 'dwelling'. It first meant a temporary shelter of boughs or tents, later a market stall.
hints: A phone one was once a street fixture.
Where you cast your vote privately.

definition: Treasure taken as loot.
note: From Middle English, from Old French butin and Middle Low German bute, 'share, loot'. Its later slang sense is separate and informal.
hints: What pirates go after.
Plunder carried off from a defeated enemy.

definition: Alcoholic drink.
note: Originally a Northern English dialect form of bowse, a word for drinking deeply. It has been slang for liquor for centuries.
hints: A bottle shop sells it by the bottle.
Casual word for what you drink at a party.

definition: Drinking a lot of alcohol, or full of it.
note: Built from booze plus -y, the adjective ending. It describes people or occasions.
hints: A long and rowdy lunch might be called this.
A drink with plenty of spirits in it.

definition: A white mineral salt used in cleaning and glassmaking.
note: Through Medieval Latin and Old French from Arabic bawraq, which itself came from Persian. The mineral was traded across the medieval world.
hints: A laundry booster sold in boxes.
A salt of boric acid found in dry lake beds.

definition: The chest, or a person's closest circle.
note: From Old English bosm, a very old Germanic word. We hold things close to it, which is how it came to mean one's inner feelings.
hints: A very close pal is called a buddy of this sort.
A mother holds a baby against hers.

definition: Fond of ordering other people around.
note: Built from boss, which came from Dutch baas, 'master', plus -y. It is an informal way of saying domineering.
hints: The sort of older sibling who gives all the orders.
Unwanted attitude on a group project.

definition: To do something badly or clumsily.
note: From Middle English bocchen, 'to mend', of uncertain origin. It first meant to patch up, and mending done carelessly gave us the modern meaning.
hints: A poor repair job is this.
A word for ruining a task by sloppy work.

definition: A large branch of a tree.
note: From Old English bog, 'shoulder, arm', which shows the branch was compared to a limb of the body. The spelling is a tricky one.
hints: A cradle in the lullaby falls when it breaks.
Heavy with fruit or snow.

definition: The intestine, or the deep inner part of something.
note: From Old French, from Latin botellus, 'little sausage'. It also names deep inner parts, as in 'the ___s of the ship'.
hints: Part of the digestive tract below the stomach.
Doctors screen it for cancer.

definition: A person who fights in a ring wearing gloves.
note: Simply box plus -er. The dog breed was named for the way it seems to spar with its front paws.
hints: Muhammad Ali was a famous one.
A breed of dog with a squashed nose and drooping jowls.

definition: To prepare for something unpleasant; or a support.
note: From Old French brace, 'arm', from Latin bracchium. Arms hold things tight, so the word came to mean a support or a prop.
hints: What you do before an impact on a plane.
Some people wear one on their teeth.

definition: To weave three strands of hair together.
note: From Old English bregdan, which meant sudden movement, pulling or weaving. The sense of interweaving remained.
hints: A hairstyle with three woven strands.
Also a decorative cord sewn onto uniforms.

definition: A device that slows or stops a vehicle.
note: Of uncertain origin, possibly from a Middle Dutch word for a curb. Many other unrelated things share the spelling.
hints: Press the pedal and the car does this.
Bicycles have hand levers for it.

definition: Loud, bold and tactless.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from a Scots word for a violent onset or attack.
hints: Not a quiet type at all.
A young hotshot who talks over everyone.

definition: A yellow alloy of copper and zinc; also trumpets and trombones.
note: From Old English bræs, of uncertain origin. Instruments made of the metal came to be a section of an orchestra.
hints: Trumpets and trombones belong to this section.
Doorknobs are often made of it.

definition: Ready to face danger without fear.
note: From Middle French, borrowed from Italian bravo. It once meant splendid or fine as well as courageous.
hints: Firefighters are said to be this.
The opposite of cowardly.

definition: A shout of praise for a performance.
note: Borrowed from Italian, where it means 'good' or 'skilled'. It shares an origin with the word brave.
hints: Audiences shout it at the end of an opera.
Also the word for the letter B in the radio alphabet.

definition: A noisy fight, usually involving many people.
note: From Middle English braulen, 'to clamour or quarrel', of otherwise uncertain origin.
hints: A pub fight often turns into one.
Messier than a scuffle.

definition: A baked food made from flour and water.
note: From Old English bread, a Germanic word. It once meant a piece or morsel, and loaf was the word for the whole.
hints: A baker's chief product.
Slice it for toast or a sandwich.

definition: To split into pieces, or to stop for a rest.
note: From Old English brecan, a very old Germanic verb. It has also come to mean a pause, a lucky chance and a dawn.
hints: What a dropped plate does.
A short rest from work.

definition: To produce young; or a type of animal.
note: From Old English bredan, related to brood. A kind of animal came to be named for how it was bred.
hints: A poodle is one type of dog this way.
Farmers do it with cattle.

definition: A thorny, tangled shrub such as a wild rose.
note: From Old English brer, of unknown further origin. Pipe makers use the wood of a related plant.
hints: Br'er Rabbit was famously thrown into a patch of it.
A thorny tangle that snags your clothes.

definition: A hard block of baked clay used for building.
note: From Middle Low German and Middle Dutch bricke, originally a broken piece or tile. The word came to mean a whole block.
hints: The house of the second pig was made of it.
Red blocks stacked with mortar.

definition: A woman on her wedding day.
note: From Old English bryd, a Germanic word that has meant a woman about to marry for well over a thousand years.
hints: Walks down the aisle in white.
Throws a bouquet after the ceremony.

definition: Short in time or in words.
note: From Latin brevis, 'short', through Old French. A legal summary and a set of lawyer's instructions took the name because they were short documents.
hints: A short summary given before a meeting.
Underwear style that is cut short.

definition: Very salty water.
note: From Old English brine, a Germanic word for salt water. It later also named the sea itself in poetry.
hints: Pickles are kept in it.
A cucumber soaks in this to become a pickle.

definition: To carry something to a place.
note: From Old English bringan, a very old Germanic verb meaning to carry or lead toward the speaker.
hints: The opposite of take.
Fetch something and come back with it.

definition: The edge of something steep, or the point just before a change.
note: From Middle English, from Old Norse, meaning the edge of a hill or slope. We now use it for the edge of dramatic events.
hints: Someone on this of tears is about to cry.
A cliff has one; so does a crisis.

definition: Salty, like seawater.
note: From brine plus -y. It often describes the taste of oysters or the smell of the sea. Poets also use it as a name for the ocean itself.
hints: What the sea tastes like.
A pickle or an olive has this flavour.

definition: Wide, from side to side.
note: From Old English brad, a very old Germanic word. It also came to mean general, as in 'in broad terms'.
hints: Shoulders on a swimmer might be this.
In the daylight, as in 'in ___ daylight'.

definition: To cook with strong direct heat from above.
note: From Middle English, from Old French bruller, 'to burn'. Another sense is a noisy quarrel, from a different word.
hints: Something an American oven can do at its top setting.
To grill under a hot element.

definition: To worry or sulk; also a group of young birds.
note: From Old English brod, 'breeding, hatching'. The hen sitting over her eggs became a picture of someone sitting and thinking over a problem.
hints: A hen with chicks has one.
What a moody person does alone.

definition: A long-handled brush for sweeping.
note: From Old English brom, 'brushwood'. The household tool took its name from the twigs of a shrub once used to make it.
hints: A witch rides one in stories.
Used to sweep the kitchen floor.

definition: A thin soup made by simmering meat or vegetables in water.
note: From Old English broth, from a Germanic word related to brewing. It is the liquid left after boiling food.
hints: Chicken soup starts with it.
Too many cooks can spoil it, the proverb says.

definition: The colour of chocolate or soil.
note: From Old English brun, a Germanic word. The colour was so named long before it was a name for a bear.
hints: Colour of a typical bear.
Mix red, yellow and blue and you get this.

definition: The worst part of an impact or attack.
note: From Middle English, meaning a sudden blow or attack. We still speak of bearing it, as the person who takes the hardest hit.
hints: Usually 'bears' or 'takes' comes before it.
The heaviest part of a storm or criticism.

definition: A tool with bristles; or to touch lightly in passing.
note: The noun is from Old French and ultimately a word for bristle. A second, separate sense names thick undergrowth.
hints: What you do to your teeth twice a day.
An artist dips one in paint.

definition: A cruel, savage person; also an animal.
note: From Latin brutus, 'dull, stupid, unfeeling', through French. It first described beasts that lack reason.
hints: '___ force' means strength without cleverness.
A thuggish bully.

definition: A friend or companion.
note: First seen about 1788, of uncertain origin. It may be a child's version of brother.
hints: Someone you might go to the gym with.
Another casual word for pal or mate.

definition: To move slightly.
note: Through Old French bouger, from Latin bullire, 'to boil, bubble'. Movement and bubbling seem to have shared an origin.
hints: A stubborn donkey won't do it.
Said of a door that is stuck fast.

definition: A small light carriage or vehicle; or full of faults.
note: Origin unknown for the carriage sense. The adjective means infested with insects or, of software, full of faults.
hints: A baby might be pushed in one.
Software that crashes often is called this.

definition: A small brass horn with no valves.
note: From Middle English, from Anglo-Norman bugle, 'young ox'. It was named for the wild ox's horn from which the earliest ones were made.
hints: Soldiers wake to its call.
Taps is played on one.

definition: To make something by putting parts together.
note: From Old English bytlan, 'to build', from a word for a dwelling. It is a very old word for making houses.
hints: Construction workers do it.
Make a house from bricks, perhaps.

definition: A swelling that sticks out.
note: Through Old French, from Latin bulga, 'leather bag', itself from a Gaulish word. A bulging bag is a good picture of it.
hints: A stuffed pocket makes one.
A battle in the Ardennes was named for a famous one.

definition: Large and awkward to carry.
note: From bulk plus -y. It is used for things that take up a lot of space without being necessarily heavy.
hints: A winter coat might be called this.
Hard to fit through a door.

definition: Someone who picks on weaker people.
note: In 1530 it was a term of endearment, perhaps from Dutch boel, 'lover, brother'. Over time it changed to mean someone who is a blustering tyrant.
hints: A playground tormentor.
What you call someone who picks on smaller kids.

definition: A group of things clustered together.
note: From Middle English bunche, 'hump, swelling', of uncertain origin. It was first a lump before it was a cluster.
hints: Grapes grow in one.
Flowers tied together make one.

definition: A rabbit, especially a young one.
note: Formed from a Scottish word, bun, meaning a rabbit's tail, with the -y of affection. It is a pet name.
hints: The Easter one hides eggs.
A fluffy animal with long ears.

definition: Large, strong and heavily built.
note: From Middle English, where it first meant 'tall, stately'. It slowly shifted from grand to brawny.
hints: A bouncer might be this.
A lumberjack's typical build.

definition: To break open suddenly.
note: From Old English berstan, a very old Germanic verb. It describes sudden breaking from pressure.
hints: What a balloon does when pricked.
A pipe in winter might do this.

definition: Thick and spreading like a bush.
note: From bush plus -y. It is most often used of eyebrows, beards and tails.
hints: A squirrel's tail is described this way.
Unclipped eyebrows might be this.

definition: A steep isolated hill with a flat top.
note: Borrowed from French, where it means a mound. It is common in the American West, where French trappers named many landforms.
hints: Monument Valley is full of them.
Smaller than a mesa.

definition: A person who purchases something.
note: From buy plus -er. It also names a professional who selects goods for a shop.
hints: The opposite of seller.
'___ beware' warns of a risky purchase.

definition: A rule made by a local authority or organisation.
note: From Middle English bilawe, partly from Old Norse byjar-log, 'town law'. The by- originally meant a village.
hints: The council passed one about noisy parties.
A rule a club or company writes for itself.

definition: A small secret group plotting together.
note: From French cabale, from Medieval Latin, from Hebrew qabbalah, 'tradition, received teaching'. It took on political meanings in 1600s England.
hints: A hidden group scheming in the shadows.
Conspirators might form one.

definition: A small wooden house, or a room on a ship or plane.
note: From Old French cabane, from Medieval Latin capanna, 'hut'. It is the same source as cabana.
hints: Log houses in the woods are called this.
Where the passengers sit on a plane.

definition: A thick rope or wire.
note: From Old French, from Late Latin capulum, 'rope, halter'. Today it also names a bundle of electrical wire or a TV service.
hints: A bridge may hang from huge steel ones.
Plug your phone into one to charge.

definition: The tree whose seeds are used to make chocolate.
note: From Spanish, from Nahuatl cacahuatl. The word cocoa is a variant of the same word.
hints: Chocolate begins as its beans.
Aztecs prized its seeds as a drink.

definition: A hidden store of things; or saved data for fast access.
note: From French cacher, 'to hide'. French-Canadian trappers used it for hiding places for supplies.
hints: A web browser clears it to free space.
Squirrels keep one of nuts for winter.

definition: A small box for tea; or a golfer's assistant.
note: The tea box name comes from kati, a Malay weight, via a pack of tea. The golf helper is a different word, from cadet.
hints: Carries clubs around a golf course.
A box on a table holding tea bags.

definition: A young person training to be an officer.
note: From French, from Gascon capdet, 'little head or chief'. It first meant a younger son, who would not inherit the family estate.
hints: Trained at a military academy.
A trainee officer in uniform.

definition: Cautious and unwilling to give information.
note: Originally American slang, of unknown origin. Some link it to the guarded behaviour of caged animals.
hints: Asked a direct question, he gave a guarded answer.
Evasive when pressed for details.

definition: A pile of stones used as a marker.
note: From Scottish Gaelic carn, from an old Celtic root. They mark graves, paths and mountain summits.
hints: Hikers stack stones to build one.
A small scottish terrier shares the name.

definition: A large desert animal with humps.
note: Through Old English and Old French from Latin camelus, from Greek, from a Semitic source. The word is related to the Arabic word jamal.
hints: One with two humps is called Bactrian.
Known for going long without water.

definition: A brief appearance by a famous person in a film.
note: From Italian cammeo, a carved gem in relief. The film sense is short for 'cameo role', a small part that stands out like a jewel.
hints: Hitchcock did this in his own films.
Also a carved brooch with a profile on it.

definition: A man-made waterway.
note: From Latin canalis, 'channel, pipe', related to canna, 'reed'. It also names a tube inside the body.
hints: Panama and Suez are famous ones.
Venice is full of them.

definition: Sweet food made with sugar.
note: From Old French sucre candi, 'candied sugar', from Arabic qandi, which came from a Persian word. The first candy was crystallised sugar.
hints: A trick-or-treater collects it.
The thing a lollipop is made of.

definition: Shrewd and careful, especially about money.
note: From a Northern English dialect word, from can in the old sense 'to know'. In Scots usage it can mean careful or lucky.
hints: A sharp-witted person with good judgment.
Good at spotting a bargain.

definition: A light, narrow boat moved with paddles.
note: Entered English in the 1500s from Spanish canoa, which took it from the Taino word for a dugout boat. It was one of the first Caribbean words Europeans borrowed.
hints: Paddled across a calm lake.
Kayak's open-topped cousin.

definition: An accepted body of rules or works.
note: From Latin canon, from Greek kanon, 'measuring rod, rule'. A rod for measuring became a standard for judging.
hints: Sacred texts accepted by a church form one.
The official set of stories in a fictional universe.

definition: A unit of weight for gemstones.
note: From Italian and Arabic qirat, itself from Greek keration, 'carob seed, small weight'. Carob seeds were once used to weigh gems.
hints: A diamond ring is measured in it.
Gold purity is measured in a related spelling.

definition: Goods carried by a ship, plane or truck.
note: Borrowed from Spanish cargo, 'load, burden', from cargar, 'to load'. It is a close relative of the word charge.
hints: What a freighter hauls.
Shipping containers are packed with it.

definition: A fixed social class one is born into.
note: From Portuguese or Spanish casta, 'lineage, breed'. Europeans applied it to the hereditary classes of Indian society.
hints: A rigid hereditary social division.
Also a word for a class of ants or bees, such as workers.

definition: To grab something thrown or moving.
note: From Old Northern French cachier and Latin captare, 'to chase', a relative of capere, 'to take'. It once meant to chase before it meant to seize.
hints: Mitt in baseball does this to a ball.
A hidden drawback, as in 'what's the ___?'

definition: To provide food and drink for an event.
note: From Middle English catour, a shortened form of acatour, 'buyer', from Old French acater, 'to buy'. A caterer was once simply a buyer of provisions.
hints: What a company does for a wedding reception.
To supply for a need, as in 'to ___ to every taste'.

definition: Subtly spiteful.
note: From cat plus -y. Cats were long thought of as sly and sharp, so a catty remark has hidden claws.
hints: A remark with a hidden sting.
Gossip that's spiteful rather than kind.

definition: A waterproof filler used to seal gaps.
note: From Old Northern French cauquer, from Late Latin calicare, 'to fill with limestone', from calx. Ship builders used it to seal the seams between planks.
hints: Seals the gaps around a bathtub.
Sold in tubes and squeezed from a gun.

definition: A thing that makes something happen.
note: Borrowed from Old French cause, from Latin causa, 'reason, sake, lawsuit'. It once also meant a legal case.
hints: The opposite of effect.
What you fight for if you are an activist.

definition: To raise petty objections.
note: From Old French caviller, from Latin cavillari, 'to jeer, to reason captiously'. It has long meant a nitpicking complaint.
hints: A fussy complaint about something trivial.
What a nitpicker does over small details.

definition: To stop.
note: From Old French cesser, from Latin cessare, 'to stop, delay'. It is usually seen in formal wording like 'cease and desist'.
hints: What a ___-fire does to the fighting.
A formal word for stop.

definition: A tall evergreen tree with fragrant wood.
note: From Latin cedrus, from Greek kedros. The scented wood is used to line chests and closets.
hints: Moths avoid its scent in a wardrobe.
Lebanon's flag shows one.

definition: A large stringed instrument played upright between the knees.
note: Short for violoncello, Italian for 'little violone', where violone was a kind of big viol. Cello was a clipped form.
hints: Bigger than a violin but smaller than a double bass.
Played sitting down with a bow.

definition: To rub and make sore.
note: From Old French chaufer, 'to warm', from Latin calefacere. Rubbing makes heat, and so the meaning shifted from warm to irritate.
hints: What a tight collar does to your neck.
To be annoyed by restrictions.

definition: The husks separated from grain.
note: From Old English ceaf, a Germanic word. 'Separating the wheat from this' means sorting good from worthless.
hints: What's blown away when grain is threshed.
Worthless stuff set apart from the wheat.

definition: A series of connected metal links.
note: From Old French chaine, from Latin catena. It names a bicycle part, a shop group and a connected series of events.
hints: A bicycle has one that goes around the cogs.
A set of linked rings, or a group of shops.

definition: A seat with a back, for one person.
note: From Old French chaiere, from Latin cathedra, from Greek kathedra, 'seat'. The same Greek word gave us cathedral.
hints: Sits at the dinner table.
Also what a person running a meeting is called.

definition: A soft white rock or a stick used for writing on boards.
note: From Old English cealc, from Latin calx, 'limestone'. The white cliffs of Dover are made of it.
hints: A teacher once used it on a blackboard.
Rock gymnasts rub on their hands.

definition: To repeat words rhythmically.
note: From Old French chanter, from Latin cantare, 'to sing'. It is a close relative of cant.
hints: What a football crowd does in unison.
Monks do this in a monotone.

definition: Complete disorder.
note: From Greek khaos, 'abyss, void'. The Greeks used it for the empty state before the world was ordered.
hints: A kitchen with a dozen cooks and no plan.
The opposite of order.

definition: The power to delight others; or a magic spell.
note: From Old French charme, from Latin carmen, 'song, incantation'. Spells were sung before they were attractions.
hints: A lucky one hangs on a bracelet.
'Third time lucky' is said to work like one.

definition: To run after something in order to catch it.
note: From Old French chacier, from Latin captare, a relative of capere, 'to take'. It is a cousin of catch.
hints: A dog does it to a squirrel.
Cars do it in action movies.

definition: A deep gap or crack in the ground.
note: From Latin chasma, from Greek khasma, 'abyss, cleft'. It also names a wide gulf between people.
hints: What a bridge is built over.
A deep gorge in the earth.

definition: Low in price.
note: From Old English ceap, 'trade, market, value', which is the root of a word for market in many languages. Originally 'good cheap' meant a good bargain.
hints: The opposite of expensive.
Might also describe poor quality.

definition: To break the rules to gain an advantage.
note: From Middle English acheten, a variant of escheten, from the legal word escheat, the seizure of property that falls to the crown. Officers who did the seizing had a reputation for dishonesty.
hints: What a student does by copying an exam.
To win unfairly.

definition: To examine to make sure something is right.
note: Ultimately from Persian shah, 'king', via the chess call of 'check' to the king. It then spread to mean stopping or testing.
hints: Said when the king is threatened in chess.
What you do to an answer before you hand it in.

definition: The soft part of the face below the eye.
note: From Old English ceace, 'jaw'. Cheeky behaviour was named for the impudent way of making faces.
hints: A kiss on the face lands here.
A hamster stuffs food into them.

definition: A board game with kings, queens and pawns.
note: From Old French esches, from the plural of eschec, 'check', from Persian shah, 'king'. The name of the game is simply 'kings'.
hints: Played on sixty-four squares.
The game where you try to checkmate.

definition: The front of the body between the neck and stomach; or a strong box.
note: From Old English cest, 'box, coffin', from Latin cista. The body part was named as the box that holds the heart and lungs.
hints: Pirates buried treasure in one.
Where your ribs are.

definition: A baby bird, especially a chicken.
note: From Middle English chike, a variant of chiken. The informal word for a young woman came later.
hints: It hatches from an egg.
Fluffy and yellow in spring.

definition: To scold mildly.
note: From Old English cidan, 'to quarrel, complain'. It carries a gentler, more old-fashioned tone than scold.
hints: A parent might do this to a child who is rude.
To rebuke gently.

definition: A leader or head of a group.
note: From Old French chef, from Latin caput, 'head'. It is a cousin of the word cap and captain.
hints: The head of a tribe or a fire department.
Main, as in 'the ___ reason'.

definition: A young human who is not yet an adult.
note: From Old English cild, from a Germanic word that may have meant 'womb'. The plural, children, keeps an odd old ending.
hints: A boy or girl.
Plays in the playground.

definition: A hot pepper, or a stew made with it.
note: Borrowed from Spanish chile, from Nahuatl chilli. The spelling varies, as in chilli or chile.
hints: A spicy pod that makes your mouth burn.
A stew of beans and meat served in a bowl.

definition: A bell-like ringing sound.
note: From Middle English, possibly from Old French chimbe, 'cymbal', from Latin cymbalum. It first named the cymbal-like sound of bells.
hints: A doorbell might play one.
To join in, as in 'to ___ in'.

definition: A short, sharp bird sound.
note: From Middle English, imitative of the sound. It is often used of birds and crickets.
hints: What a cricket does at night.
A small bird's morning sound.

definition: A wedge placed to stop something moving.
note: From Old Northern French choque, 'block, log'. It is used for wheels, boats and barrels.
hints: Put behind the wheel of a parked aircraft.
A wedge that stops a wheel rolling.

definition: A group of singers performing together.
note: From Old French quer, from Latin chorus, 'dance, band of singers'. The spelling changed to resemble the Latin.
hints: Sings carols at Christmas.
Part of a church where singers stand.

definition: To be unable to breathe because something blocks the throat.
note: From Old English aceocian, 'to choke'. It also means to panic and fail under pressure.
hints: What a bite of food might make you do.
To fail under pressure, like a golfer on the last hole.

definition: A routine household task.
note: From earlier char, Middle English for an odd job or turn, from Old English cierr, 'a turn'. The meaning of a small daily job stuck.
hints: Taking out the rubbish is one.
Something children are assigned for pocket money.

definition: To throw carelessly.
note: A variant of chock, meaning a block or lump. As a verb it came to mean toss, and the cut of beef is the same word.
hints: What you do to an old shoe in the bin.
Part of a drill that holds the bit.

definition: A fool, or someone easily tricked.
note: Of uncertain origin, perhaps a blend of chunk and lump. It first meant a blockhead.
hints: A sucker taken in by a scam.
'Don't be a ___,' you might tell a friend.

definition: A thick, solid piece.
note: A variant of chuck, perhaps from chump, with a diminutive ending. It names a thick piece of something.
hints: A big lump of cheese.
A large portion of your salary.

definition: A slide or sloping channel.
note: Borrowed directly from French chute, 'fall'. It is also a short form of parachute.
hints: A playground slide, or a laundry or rubbish passage.
A sloping channel for sliding things down.

definition: A roll of tobacco leaves for smoking.
note: From Spanish cigarro, of uncertain origin. It is often smoked on special occasions.
hints: Handed out in celebration when a baby is born.
Rolled tobacco that is thicker than a smoke in a paper tube.

definition: Something very easy; or a strap on a saddle.
note: From Spanish cincha, 'girth, belt', from Latin cingulum. A tightly fastened strap became a sure thing.
hints: A sure thing, or something simple.
A strap that holds a saddle on a horse.

definition: Around; approximately, used with dates.
note: Borrowed from Latin circa, 'around', related to circus and circle. Historians write it, often as 'c.', before an uncertain date.
hints: Seen before a date on a museum label.
Abbreviated c. in front of a year.

definition: Relating to a city or its citizens.
note: Borrowed from Latin civicus, 'of a citizen', from civis, 'citizen'. A citizen's duties came to be called civic duties.
hints: Voting is considered a duty of this kind.
A town hall is a ___ building.

definition: Polite, or relating to ordinary citizens.
note: From Old French and Latin civilis, 'relating to a citizen', from civis. It contrasts with military or religious matters, and with rude behaviour.
hints: What a courteous but cold conversation might be.
A ___ war is fought between citizens of one country.

definition: A short, sharp, hard sound.
note: From Middle English clacken, imitative of the noise. It is the sound of two hard things repeatedly knocking.
hints: Heels do it on a tile floor.
Typewriter keys make this noise.

definition: To say that something is true or yours.
note: From Old French clamer, 'to call out', from Latin clamare, 'to cry out'. A claim was once literally a calling out of what you owned.
hints: A miner might stake one.
An insurance customer files one.

definition: A device that grips things tightly together.
note: From Middle Dutch clampe, 'hook', from a Germanic root related to clasp. It is a tool for holding.
hints: A carpenter holds two boards together with one.
A parking wheel lock is also called this.

definition: A loud ringing metallic sound.
note: From about 1570, imitative of the sound. It resembles the German word Klang.
hints: What a dropped pan does on a tile floor.
A bell strikes it, but harshly.

definition: A dull heavy metallic sound.
note: Imitative of the sound itself. It is lower and heavier than a clang.
hints: Chains drag across the floor with this noise.
A knight's armour makes it as he walks.

definition: To crash together noisily, or to conflict.
note: Imitative, like crash and smash. It came to mean fights and also colours that do not match.
hints: Two armies meet in one.
Orange and pink might do this.

definition: To grip tightly; or a fastener.
note: From Middle English claspe, a metal catch or hook. The noun and the verb have been in use since the 1300s.
hints: A necklace has one at the back.
To hold hands tightly.

definition: A group of students; or a category or rank.
note: From French classe and Latin classis, a division of Roman citizens. It grew to mean any group sorted by rank or type.
hints: Students sit in it at school.
A social rank, like middle or working.

definition: Free from dirt.
note: From Old English clæne, meaning pure or clear. It once described moral purity too.
hints: What you make a room before guests arrive.
The opposite of dirty.

definition: Easy to see through, or easy to understand.
note: From Old French cler, from Latin clarus, 'bright, clear'. It describes light, water, and ideas alike.
hints: A window pane that is spotless is this.
Describes skies with no clouds.

definition: A wedge or strip used for gripping or fastening.
note: From Middle English clete, meaning a wedge or block. Shoes and boats both have them.
hints: A soccer boot has studs of this kind.
A sailor ties a rope around one on the dock.

definition: A split or crack, such as in a chin.
note: From Middle English clift, related to cleave. It names a gap made by splitting.
hints: A dimple in a person's chin is called this.
'In a ___ stick' means trapped in a split in wood.

definition: An office or shop worker who keeps records or serves customers.
note: From Old English clerc, from Late Latin clericus, 'priest, learned man'. Churchmen were once the only ones who could write, so clerk meant scribe.
hints: Takes your payment at a hotel desk.
A shop assistant who rings up sales.

definition: A short, sharp sound; or to press a mouse button.
note: Imitative of the sound, first recorded in the 1500s. Computer use gave it a new life.
hints: What a mouse does when pressed.
The sound a light switch makes.

definition: A steep rock face.
note: From Old English clif, a Germanic word. It named the seaside rock long before the figurative cliff-edge.
hints: The white ones at Dover look over the sea.
A dangerous place to stand near the edge.

definition: To go up using hands and feet.
note: From Old English climban, from a Germanic root. The b was once pronounced and is now silent.
hints: What you do on a ladder.
Mountaineers do this to reach summits.

definition: To hold on tightly.
note: From Old English clingan, 'to adhere, stick together'. It is often used for wet clothes and for people afraid to let go.
hints: A koala does this to a tree.
Wet fabric might do this to skin.

definition: A light ringing sound of glass or metal touching.
note: From Middle English clinken, imitative of the sound. It is also old slang for prison.
hints: The sound when glasses touch in a toast.
Coins in a pocket make it.

definition: An exact genetic copy of an organism.
note: Coined in botany in 1903 from Greek klon, 'twig'. Plants grown from cuttings were the first clones.
hints: Dolly the sheep was one.
An identical copy of something.

definition: To shut.
note: From Middle English closen, from Old French clos, from Latin clausus. It is a familiar word with several distinct senses.
hints: What you do to a door.
Nearby, as in 'a ___ friend'.

definition: A visible mass of water droplets in the sky.
note: From Old English clud, which meant 'rock, hill'. The mass of rain-bearing vapour was likened to a hill in the sky.
hints: It rains from this when it's grey.
A fluffy white one drifts overhead.

definition: A dried flower bud used as a spice; or a segment of garlic.
note: From Old French clou de girofle, 'nail of the clove tree', since the bud looks like a small nail.
hints: A bud used to stud a ham.
One segment of a bulb of garlic.

definition: A performer in baggy clothes and a red nose.
note: From earlier clowne, 'a rustic, a boor', likely from a Scandinavian source. The meaning shifted from a clumsy peasant to a comic performer.
hints: A circus performer with a red nose.
Someone who acts silly to get laughs.

definition: The noise a hen makes.
note: From Old English cloccian, imitative of the hen's sound. It can also describe a sound of disapproval.
hints: A mother hen calls her chicks with it.
What you do with your tongue to show disapproval.

definition: A tight cluster or lump.
note: From Old English clympre, 'lump or mass of metal', from a Germanic root. It describes things bunched together.
hints: Grass growing in a tuft.
Hair stuck together in a wet mass.

definition: A trainer; or a large carriage or bus.
note: The carriage named for Kocs, a Hungarian town, is a popular theory. It later meant a tutor who carries a student through an exam.
hints: Leads a sports team from the sideline.
A fancy horse-drawn carriage in a fairy tale.

definition: The land along the sea.
note: From Old French coste, 'rib, side, coast'. The word first meant a side of the body.
hints: Where the land meets the ocean.
To glide without effort, as a bicycle down a hill.

definition: A venomous snake that spreads a hood.
note: From Portuguese cobra, from Latin colubra, 'female snake'. It rears up and flattens its neck when threatened.
hints: Snake charmers play to one.
Rudyard Kipling's Rikki-Tikki-Tavi fights one.

definition: A powder made from cacao seeds; a hot chocolate drink.
note: From Spanish cacao, via Nahuatl. Cocoa came from confusing the word with coco, a spelling Johnson's dictionary helped spread.
hints: Hot drink with marshmallows.
Powder used in baking chocolate cake.

definition: The punctuation mark that looks like two dots; also part of the bowel.
note: From Latin colon and Greek kolon, 'limb, clause'. The mark was named for a member of a sentence, the bowel for a different Greek word.
hints: Written before a list.
Two dots stacked on top of each other.

definition: The quality of light that makes red, blue and green different.
note: From Old French color, from Latin color, 'colour, hue'. Spelled colour in British English.
hints: Red or blue, for example.
A crayon box is full of them.

definition: Cosy and comfortable.
note: A shortening of comfortable plus -y, dating to the early 1800s. It is a casual, affectionate word.
hints: How a favourite old sweater feels.
A cosy armchair is described this way.

definition: Funny; or a person or book that's funny.
